output.brief: The evidence points mainly to the revised merit scholarship schedule, not the Admissions Office. Yield fell sharply only in the tiers whose awards were cut: Dean's from 45.2% to 31.9% and Merit from 44.9% to 32.3%. Presidential awards were unchanged and yield held at about 36%. No-award admits barely moved, from 38.5% to 37.0%. Applications and admit quality rose, so the applicant pool is not the problem. Early-action yield also fell, from 45.2% to 37.8%, even though those admits got decisions on the old timetable. So slow regular-decision turnaround cannot explain the whole drop. It probably cost some students, as the counsellor's email shows, but its size is unmeasured. Missing documents on the portal are unconfirmed. Replacing the director would punish the wrong party and would not address the main cause. Next step: take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the net-revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Separately, set a regular-decision turnaround target and fix reviewer staffing. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the transcript issue is checked. I'm fairly confident in the scholarship finding. The size of the turnaround effect is the main remaining gap.
